title: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
desc: Demands realistic, task-specific and reproducible legal-AI evaluation rather than exam scores, fluency or model-name comparisons.

kps.k: The central proposition is to measure legal AI against specific professional tasks, not infer practical competence from exam scores or fluent answers.
kps.d: LegalBench separates distinct reasoning skills into expert-designed tasks; Harvey’s BigLaw Bench evaluates document-based work products; LAB extends testing to multi-step assignments involving document discovery, tool use and complete deliverables. These approaches measure different capabilities rather than interchangeable versions of legal intelligence. Harvey reports 1,250 LAB tasks across 24 practice areas, but acknowledges incomplete coverage. Jon Choi’s criticism goes further: even professional benchmarks underrepresent ambiguous, strategic problems without a single correct answer. Gabe Pereyra counters that much large-firm work supports meaningful task-level measurement, without claiming that all legal judgment is quantifiable.

qs.q: The second challenge is the incongruity between the ways in which existing benchmarks and lawyers frame “legal reasoning.” Existing benchmarks coarsely generalize all tasks involving legal data or laws as measuring “legal reasoning.” In contrast, lawyers recognize that legal reasoning is a broad umbrella term encompassing many distinct types of reasoning [47].
qs.a: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models · Academia · 2023

qs.q: -  **Output: **To complete tasks successfully, the agent must produce reviewable legal work product.
qs.a: Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB): Official Announcement, Repository, Methodology, and Initial Results · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: High partial-credit scores can coexist with low rates of complete legal-task success.
kps.d: LAB requires every rubric criterion to pass, on Harvey’s rationale that one omitted risk can make a deliverable materially incomplete. Harvey’s May 26, 2026 initial results put the leading configuration, Opus 4.7, at 7.1% all-pass. Artificial Analysis’s separate July 7 implementation reports 14.2% for Fable 5 at maximum reasoning, with an Opus 4.8 fallback on one task, despite a 93.6% criterion pass rate. Vals separately reports 55.29% all-pass versus 90.58% weighted credit for Opus 5 on Legal Research Bench. These results illustrate the completion gap, not a common ranking or a directly comparable progress series. BigLaw Bench’s earlier 74% work-product score likewise does not mean 74% autonomous task completion.

qs.q: Importantly, a task is marked complete only if every criterion passes, a concept we refer to as **all-pass grading**.
qs.a: Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB): Official Announcement, Repository, Methodology, and Initial Results · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: Claude Opus 4.7 leads at 7.1%, with Sonnet 4.6 at 5.4%, Opus 4.6 at 4.2%, GPT-5.5 at 2.1%, and Gemini 3.5 Flash at 0.
qs.a: Initial Results on Legal Agent Benchmark: A First Look at Frontier Model Performance on Long-Horizon Legal-Agent Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: The definition and grading of legal quality remain contested.
kps.d: Strict all-pass scoring emphasizes completeness; Legora BAR instead weights requirements by stakeholder risk and penalizes consequential omissions; Allens uses scaled expert marks to capture nuance and variability. JudgmentBench enables comparison of rubric and preference assessments by the same experts on the same outputs, but the supplied material establishes no superior method. Automated judges offer scale, yet require validation: Vals reports 87.4% agreement with a three-expert majority for its research judge, versus an 83.4% average individual-human baseline. That measures grading agreement, not direct human review of every response or proof of legal correctness. Harvey also distinguishes substantive quality from accurate source traceability, which supports—but does not replace—human verification.

qs.q: They draw knowledge from their expertise, and mark rubrics as high/medium/low importance dependent on how much risk the deliverable exposes its stakeholders to if the rubric was not met.
qs.a: Introducing the Legora BAR — The Legora Benchmark for Agentic Reasoning · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: To our knowledge, it is the first publicly available expert-annotated legal benchmark in which the same outputs are evaluated under both rubric-based and comparative-judgment protocols, enabling direct comparison of the two methodologies on shared, high-judgment legal work products.
qs.a: JudgmentBench: Comparing Rubric and Preference Evaluation for Quality Assessment · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Benchmark results depend on the tested system and protocol, not just the model name.
kps.d: Artificial Analysis simplifies tools and prompts to target raw model ability, while Legora argues that testing inside its deployed harness better represents customer experience. Harvey, Artificial Analysis and Applied Compute also use different grading arrangements. LegalBench reports more than 20 balanced-accuracy points of prompt variation on one task. Allens controls comparison through single prompts but explicitly excludes iterative refinement and several practical workflows. These design choices answer different questions; comparisons need disclosure of model versions, tools, prompts, reasoning effort, datasets and judges. Testing against an experienced-lawyer standard also differs from measuring human professionals completing the same tasks.

qs.q: Our benchmark evaluates models on real legal cases across practice areas, inside the Legora harness and the Legora aOS™.
qs.a: Introducing the Legora BAR — The Legora Benchmark for Agentic Reasoning · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: On overruling for instance, the best Incite-Instruct prompt improves upon the worst prompt by over 20 points (balanced-accuracy).
qs.a: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models · Academia · 2023

kps.k: Independent scrutiny and reproducibility compete with confidentiality and contamination controls.
kps.d: Ambrogi cautions that Harvey and its partners choose LAB’s tasks and definitions of good work, while explicitly rejecting vendor authorship as sufficient grounds to dismiss it. Neil Cameron questions the subjectivity and coding reliability of BigLaw Bench’s time-entry inputs. Public releases permit scrutiny, but openness varies: LAB initially exposes code and part of its data; Vals retains private tests to limit overfitting; Legora protects partner intellectual property and guards against training contamination, releasing one synthetic case. External collaboration or methodology review does not itself validate performance results. The supplied HAQQ study is explicitly low-reliability and derivative, so its results cannot supply corroborating evidence.

qs.q: The tasks and definitions of “legal work product” within LAB reflect choices about what good legal work looks like, and those choices were made by Harvey’s team in consultation with its research partners.
qs.a: Some Thoughts On Harvey's Launch of 'LAB,' An Open-Source, Long-Horizon Benchmark for Legal AI Agents · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: While attempts to normalise such data, such as 'area of law', 'work types', UTBMS and J-Codes, can provide some objective basis for comparison and analysis, these are often treated with slapdash accuracy by careless attorneys, and by more imaginative attorneys as much as a challenge to exploit for commercial purposes, as they are for support and enlightenment.
qs.a: 'The Gen AI LLM benchmarking war starts here': Harvey releases new evaluation framework · Market & press · 2024

kps.k: Benchmarks increasingly guide model development, but benchmark improvement does not establish production competence.
kps.d: Applied Compute reports raising GLM-5.1’s criterion pass rate from 85.3% to 91.3% and all-pass rate from 5.9% to 12.6% through joint grader, harness and reinforcement-learning optimization. It attributes gains partly to better tool handling, not training alone, and warns that models can exploit grader flaws. Harvey’s trajectory analysis associates self-correction, context gathering and substantive revision with success; these are correlations in agent behavior, not evidence about human verification or causal effects. Both accounts position benchmarks as development infrastructure. Applied Compute’s interpretation that the gains reflect legal competence remains distinct from demonstrated client outcomes.

qs.q: The resulting model lifts rubric pass rate from 0.853 to 0.913 and all-pass rate from 0.059 to 0.126, making it the strongest available model by rubric pass rate and second only to Opus 4.8 Max on all-pass rate.
qs.a: Training a State-of-the-Art Legal Agent with Harvey · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: We analyzed how those actions combine into behaviors and how those behaviors correlate with outcomes.
qs.a: Initial Results on Legal Agent Benchmark: A First Look at Frontier Model Performance on Long-Horizon Legal-Agent Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Task-specific quality, jurisdiction, cost and latency matter more for deployment than a universal leaderboard winner.
kps.d: Harvey’s LAB rankings change across practice-area groups, supporting its recommendation for task-sensitive model selection. Allens’ April 2025 Australian-law assessment similarly finds uneven performance despite improvement over 2024. Vals reports a pooled 11-point research-score decline when questions require reconciling conflicting authorities. Cost comparisons also resist a simple quality-price rule: Harvey’s initial leader costs about $50.90 and takes 22 minutes per task, while Artificial Analysis finds GLM-5.2 matching Opus 4.8’s completion score at roughly $1.30 rather than $8.20 per task. These are configuration-specific operating costs, not measured savings after lawyer review. Multi-model routing and cheaper adequate models are proposed deployment strategies, not established ROI findings.

qs.q: Maximizing agent performance on a real legal workload requires understanding which model family best matches the task at hand.
qs.a: Initial Results on Legal Agent Benchmark: A First Look at Frontier Model Performance on Long-Horizon Legal-Agent Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: GPT-4o, OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1 each bettered 2024's highest score (achieved by GPT-4), particularly on *substance* scores*.* - While all tested LLMs achieved good scores for some questions, the quality of the responses of all LLMs varied across the full question set.
qs.a: The 2025 Allens AI Australian law benchmark · Law firms · 2025

kps.k: The practical implication is evidence-based, supervised delegation rather than treating scores, adoption or certification as permission for autonomous legal advice.
kps.d: Harvey presents LAB as a way to distinguish work suitable for delegation with review from work requiring heavier human involvement. Allens’ February 2024 chatbot tests found no tested tool dependable for critical-reasoning advice without expert supervision; later Allens and Linklaters reports describe improvement without establishing general substitution. Ambrogi proposes practice-specific vendor comparisons, while the shared Legal AI Evaluation Framework adds organizational fit and workflow usability. Harvey’s client-ready product claims and internal lawyer testing are not independent completion measurements. Its reported AIUC-1 certification addresses agent security, safety and reliability through external scrutiny, but the supplied announcement does not establish substantive accuracy across legal tasks.

qs.q: For law firms in particular, LAB is meant to help understand which parts of a workflow can be delegated to agents, where lawyer review matters most, and what capabilities still need to improve.
qs.a: Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB): Official Announcement, Repository, Methodology, and Initial Results · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: - For tasks that involve critical reasoning, none of the tools we tested (being publicly available chatbots implementing GPT-4, Gemini 1, Claude 2, Perplexity and LLaMa 2) can be relied on to produce correct legal advice without expert human supervision.
qs.a: Lawyer or language model? Testing AI's competence in answering Australian legal questions (The Allens AI Australian Law Benchmark) · Law firms · 2024

kps.k: Public-facing legal help requires its own evaluation standards; enterprise benchmarks do not establish access-to-justice benefits.
kps.d: The Stanford Legal Design Lab material prioritizes the quality of responses to people facing civil legal problems and proposes 22 criteria reviewed by legal-help professionals. The certification scholarship likewise proposes adapting benchmark procedures to tasks important to unrepresented litigants, noting that most existing datasets support attorneys. These proposals broaden the debate from professional productivity to whether people without legal assistance receive useful, accurate help. The supplied material describes standards and intended applications, not demonstrated improvements in access to justice or reliable unsupervised advice.

qs.q: This study presents a proposed set of 22 specific criteria to evaluate the quality of a system’s answers to a person’s request for legal help for a civil justice problem.
qs.a: AI & Access to Justice Initiative — project hub (Stanford Legal Design Lab) · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Most of these datasets have been developed for training and evaluating capabilities to support attorneys’ activities.
qs.a: Certifying Legal AI Assistants for Unrepresented Litigants: A Global Survey of Access to Civil Justice, Unauthorized Practice of Law, and AI · Academia · 2024

vlens.an: The academia-and-research sources generally accept the proposition that legal AI should be evaluated through realistic, task-specific benchmarks rather than exam performance, fluency or undifferentiated claims of “legal reasoning.” They materially develop that position by supplying expert-designed legal tasks, standardized and reproducible protocols, evidence of substantial prompt sensitivity, criteria for evaluating public-facing civil legal help, and proposed accuracy standards for tasks important to unrepresented litigants. Common reasons include the mismatch between certification exams and actual use cases, the diversity of legal reasoning skills, and the need for professional experts to define legally meaningful quality. Material variation concerns scope: LegalBench focuses on differentiated reasoning capabilities; the Stanford Legal Design Lab and certification scholarship redirect evaluation toward access-to-justice tasks; and TheAgentCompany contributes a broader workplace-agent methodology while stressing limits arising from automatically gradable tasks, scaffold choice, absent human comparisons and imperfect workplace representativeness. These sources mostly propose evaluation infrastructure rather than demonstrate reliable deployment outcomes. They also do not directly substantiate the cluster’s narrower claim that partial-credit scores overstate complete legal-task success; TheAgentCompany uses partial credit but does not compare it with strict completion rates. One bibliographic excerpt is insufficient to determine any position. Because this is a curated set, this synthesis characterizes only the supplied sources and does not imply prevalence across academia or research.

qs.q: Relatedly, benchmarking efforts have focused on professional certification exams like the Uniform Bar Exam [71], but these are not always representative of the actual use-cases for LLMs.
qs.a: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models · Academia · 2023

qs.q: We identified a core set of legal tasks above that are important for unrepresented litigants and will now show how the evaluation procedures developed by the legal AI research community can establish clear standards for accuracy in AI capabilities for these tasks.
qs.a: Certifying Legal AI Assistants for Unrepresented Litigants: A Global Survey of Access to Civil Justice, Unauthorized Practice of Law, and AI · Academia · 2024

vlens.an: These selected traditional-law-firm sources accept the cluster’s principal proposition and materially develop it through jurisdiction-specific, expert-led and repeatable evaluation. Across Linklaters and Allens, the common reasoning is that fluent or comparatively strong output does not establish dependable professional competence: performance varies by question and practice area, legal nuance and jurisdictional errors require specialist assessment, and critical-reasoning outputs remain subject to expert supervision and verification. Allens’ 2025 methodology extends the proposition most concretely by using scaled, question-level human grading to expose variation that aggregate or binary scores can obscure, while also disclosing that its single-prompt protocol excludes iterative prompting and longer-form workflows. Internal variation is mainly temporal and methodological rather than directional: Allens’ 2024 assessment is more cautionary, finding no tested general-purpose chatbot reliable for unsupervised critical-reasoning advice; its 2025 report records improvement but continuing unevenness; Linklaters similarly moves from poor earlier English-law results, including fictional citations, toward a limited first-draft research-assistance role rather than autonomous substitution. Because these are curated sources, this alignment should not be generalized to traditional law firms as a whole.

qs.q: - For tasks that involve critical reasoning, none of the tools we tested (being publicly available chatbots implementing GPT-4, Gemini 1, Claude 2, Perplexity and LLaMa 2) can be relied on to produce correct legal advice without expert human supervision.
qs.a: Lawyer or language model? Testing AI's competence in answering Australian legal questions (The Allens AI Australian Law Benchmark) · Law firms · 2024

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech vendor sources collectively accept the proposition that legal AI should be evaluated on specific, realistic professional work rather than exam performance, fluency or model-name rankings, and they materially develop it through concrete evaluation infrastructure. Their principal extensions include long-horizon matter-based tasks, reviewable work products, strict all-pass or risk-weighted grading, separate measures for substantive quality and source traceability, testing of the deployed model–harness–tools system, held-out datasets, expert-judge validation, and reporting of practice-area, cost and latency differences. The strongest evidence also directly demonstrates the completion gap: high criterion-level or weighted scores can coexist with much lower whole-task success. Material internal variation concerns what should be tested and how. Harvey’s LAB emphasizes all-pass completion and supervised delegation; Legora evaluates its full production system and weights omissions by stakeholder risk; JudgmentBench compares competing expert-assessment protocols; Vals supplies independent runs and judge-agreement evidence; and LeMAJ focuses more narrowly on granular legal question-answering. Openness also varies because public scrutiny competes with confidentiality and contamination controls. Some sources redirect toward security certification or informal usefulness, while Harvey’s product launch combines task-specific internal testing with unsupported client-ready marketing claims. Vendor-built and private evaluations therefore advance the proposition methodologically but generally do not, without independent replication or client-outcome evidence, establish production competence. These findings describe only the curated sources supplied, not legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: - Under partial-credit scoring, [Claude Opus 5](/models/anthropic_claude-opus-5) reaches 90.58% weighted pass rate but 55.29% under strict all-pass grading, where every rubric check must pass.
qs.a: Vals Index — Continuous Independent Agentic Benchmark (Legal Sector: Legal Research Bench + Independent HLAB Runs) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: Legora BAR evaluates AI models across a comprehensive set of end-to-end legal tasks drawn from real-world cases, purpose-built to track how Legora performs as both the underlying models and our own harness advance over time.
qs.a: Introducing the Legora BAR — The Legora Benchmark for Agentic Reasoning · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: These selected market-analyst, consultancy and press sources broadly accept the proposition that legal AI should be evaluated on realistic, task-specific work rather than fluency, exam performance or model identity alone. They materially extend it in three ways: by demonstrating the large gap between criterion-level partial success and complete deliverables; by connecting benchmarks to supervised delegation, procurement, workflow fit, cost and model routing; and by demanding scrutiny of vendor-defined tasks, underlying data and evaluation protocols. Material variation remains. Descrybe’s vendor-run MBE study redirects toward richer exam-based reasoning tests, which detect persuasive but legally unsound analysis but still do not reproduce professional work products. Reporting on BigLaw Bench and LAB supports task-specific evaluation while questioning subjective time-entry inputs, partial openness and vendor control over definitions of quality. The shared procurement framework broadens evaluation beyond substantive output to strategic fit and workflow usability, but reports a proposed framework rather than demonstrated procurement outcomes. Harvey-focused product reporting shows benchmarks influencing system design and multi-model routing, although usage and strategy claims do not independently establish legal quality. Artificial Analysis provides the strongest direct extension through an independently specified implementation showing that high criterion pass rates coexist with rare complete-task success and that protocol and cost materially affect deployment conclusions. This characterises only the curated sources supplied, not market analysts, consultancies or the press generally.

qs.q: Frontier legal work is far from solved: most models pass a majority of individual rubric criteria but fully satisfy the requirements of very few tasks.
qs.a: Announcing Harvey LAB-AA: evaluating AI agents on real-world legal work · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: The tasks and definitions of “legal work product” within LAB reflect choices about what good legal work looks like, and those choices were made by Harvey’s team in consultation with its research partners.
qs.a: Some Thoughts On Harvey's Launch of 'LAB,' An Open-Source, Long-Horizon Benchmark for Legal AI Agents · Market & press · 2026

vlens.an: This source supports the proposition’s core demand for realistic, task-specific legal-AI evaluation. Leonard and McCormack welcome independent benchmarking that uses concrete legal workflows defined with law firms, measures output accuracy, and compares AI tools with lawyers completing the same tasks. Their reasoning is that legal work is sufficiently repeatable to permit meaningful comparison and that claims of privilege or bespoke practice should not become blanket excuses for avoiding scrutiny. The source also adds an institutional emphasis on independence from vendors. However, its support is limited in scope: the excerpt reports the study design but no performance results, ranking, reproducibility analysis, grading methodology, or evidence about the gap between partial-credit scores and complete-task success. There is little internal disagreement between the two speakers; McCormack is more emphatic and speculative about legal exceptionalism, while Leonard focuses more narrowly on the benchmark’s structure and participants. This is evidence from one curated source and should not be treated as representative of regulators, courts and professional bodies generally.

qs.q: Researchers partnered with firms like Reed Smith, Fisher Phillips, McDermott Will & Emery, and Ogletree Deakins to define tasks for the AI tools, including: Data extraction, Document Q&A, Summarization, Redlining, Transcript analysis, Chronology generation, and EDGAR research.
qs.a: Future-Proofing Your Law Firm: Lessons from AI Benchmarking — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Each tool’s output was measured for accuracy, and VALS partnered with Cognia Law—an ALSP—to source human lawyers who also completed these tasks.
qs.a: Future-Proofing Your Law Firm: Lessons from AI Benchmarking — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources collectively build the methodological foundation for the proposition. They reject exam performance, fluent output and simple model rankings as sufficient evidence of professional competence, and instead develop expert-designed, task-specific and reproducible evaluations. Harvey’s BigLaw Bench adds separate measures for substantive work product and source traceability; LegalBench shows that prompt design materially changes measured performance; TheAgentCompany makes agent environments reproducible while acknowledging partial-credit, task-selection, scaffold and representativeness limits; and Allens connects repeatable jurisdiction-specific testing to expert supervision. Material variation remains: these early benchmarks generally use partial or scaled credit and do not yet demonstrate the later, quantified gap between high criterion-level scores and low complete-task success. Harvey nevertheless distinguishes its 74% work-product measure from full completion and acknowledges incomplete coverage. The public-facing legal-assistance source extends task-specific standards to unrepresented litigants, whereas OpenAI redirects attention toward reported usefulness, commercial capability claims and lawyer review rather than reproducible completion measurement. Because this is a curated set, these positions should not be treated as representative of all sources from the period.

qs.q: Relatedly, benchmarking efforts have focused on professional certification exams like the Uniform Bar Exam [71], but these are not always representative of the actual use-cases for LLMs.
qs.a: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Harvey’s proprietary models significantly outperform publicly available LLMs, but all models show substantial room for improvement when benchmarked against full completion of tasks performed by lawyers.
qs.a: Introducing BigLaw Bench to Evaluate LLMs · Legal-tech vendor · 2024

elens.an: Across this curated 2025 source set, the evidence accepts the proposition that legal AI should be evaluated on specific professional tasks rather than inferred from exam success, fluent output or model-level averages, and materially develops that approach through jurisdiction-specific expert grading, human-lawyer baselines, granular answer assessment, contract-focused testing, public-facing civil-legal-help criteria and task-sensitive model selection. Common reasons include uneven performance across tasks and practice areas, the risk that convincing answers are wrong or incomplete, and the importance of legal nuance, citations, jurisdiction and protocol design. Material variation concerns what realistic evaluation should measure and how: Harvey emphasises workflow-step model selection and proprietary task benchmarks; Allens uses scaled expert scoring and discloses that its repeatable single-prompt protocol omits iterative and longer-form workflows; Linklaters tests specialist English-law advice while treating newer models as potential research assistants rather than substitutes; LeMAJ develops granular judging and reproducibility; independent benchmarking advocates compare tools with lawyers on firm-defined tasks; and Stanford distinguishes public-facing civil legal help from enterprise legal work. The sources do not uniformly demonstrate the synthesis’s specific claim that partial-credit scores overstate complete-task success: several use scaled or criterion-based quality measures, and some excerpts describe frameworks without reporting outcomes. One bibliographic excerpt is substantively insufficient. Overall, the period builds on the proposition by expanding task-specific evaluation methods while reinforcing that benchmark improvement does not establish autonomous production competence.

qs.q: The exam tests whether people can memorize legal rules and apply them to hypothetical situations—not whether they can exercise strategic judgment in complicated realities or craft arguments in uncharted legal territory.
qs.a: AI Might Not Be Coming for Lawyers' Jobs Anytime Soon · Market & press · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that legal AI should be evaluated on specific professional tasks rather than inferred from fluent answers, exam performance or model names, and they materially develop it with long-horizon, matter-based benchmarks, reviewable work products and strict completion measures. The strongest evidence comes from Harvey’s LAB results and independent implementations by Vals AI and Artificial Analysis: high criterion-level or weighted scores coexist with much lower all-pass rates, supporting the claim that partial credit overstates complete legal-task success. The period also broadens deployment-relevant evaluation to system harnesses and tools, practice-area and jurisdictional variation, cost, latency, procurement fit, agent trajectories and selective lawyer-supervised delegation. Material internal variation concerns how quality should be graded—strict all-pass, risk-weighted rubrics or comparative expert judgment—and how openness should be balanced against confidentiality and benchmark contamination. Vendor-run benchmarks provide useful designs and system-specific findings but not independent proof of production competence; the HAQQ results are especially unsuitable as corroboration because the source is derivative and marked low-reliability. Some sources redirect rather than directly support the proposition: Descrybe uses richer bar-exam reasoning tests, while Harvey’s AIUC-1 announcement focuses on security, safety and reliability certification rather than substantive legal-task quality. Harvey’s client-ready product announcement is mixed because task-specific internal testing aligns with the proposition, but its broad production claims lack reproducible completion evidence. These variations qualify the evidence without displacing the period’s principal contribution: concrete benchmark designs and results that strengthen the case for realistic, system-specific and supervised evaluation.

qs.q: Importantly, a task is marked complete only if every criterion passes, a concept we refer to as **all-pass grading**.
